paper_metadata.title: OPTIMIZING SYNTACTIC-SEMANTIC RELATION EXTRACTION FOR THE KAZAKH LANGUAGE WITH TRANSFORMER ARCHITECTURES AND SYNTHETIC CORPORA
paper_metadata.venue: Herald of the Kazakh-British Technical University, Vol. 23, No. 2
paper_metadata.abstract: The paper studies subject-predicate-object triple extraction for low-resource Kazakh. It generates additional training data, trains and tests XLM-RoBERTa for triple extraction, and reports an F1-score of 90.73%, arguing that synthetic-data augmentation can improve performance and support information-retrieval and knowledge-management applications.

problem_addressed: Extract SPO triples from Kazakh unstructured text despite scarce annotated corpora, agglutinative morphology, and flexible word order. The objective is to optimize a transformer-based extractor by augmenting limited real training data with GPT-4-generated Kazakh examples.

methodology.description: Execution order: (1) prompt GPT-4/ChatGPT to generate Kazakh sentences, English translations, and SPO annotations; (2) automatically filter malformed sentences, repeated tokens, and invalid BIO spans; rule-check one contiguous SPO triple; manually review a stratified subset; (3) combine limited real data with 10,000 synthetic sentences at a real:synthetic ratio of 1:2; (4) tokenize and sequentially label tokens with an XLM-RoBERTa encoder plus classification layer, Softmax, cross-entropy loss, and dropout; (5) decode BIO labels as subject, predicate, and object spans and evaluate extraction. The paper additionally lists tokenization, stemming, lemmatization, TF-IDF, Word2Vec, stop-listing, and morphological analysis as preprocessing, but does not isolate their contribution.

ontology_or_schema_use.value: No ontology or external KG schema is used. The task schema is a fixed SPO relation with BIO token labels for subject, predicate, object, and outside tokens; validation requires exactly one consistent contiguous SPO triple per generated sentence.

input_output.input_type: Kazakh natural-language sentences; synthetic examples also include an English translation and SPO annotation during data creation.
input_output.input_granularity: Sentence-level input; token-level sequence labeling within each sentence.
input_output.output_representation: One subject-predicate-object triple represented through BIO labels over sentence tokens; output spans are subject, predicate, and object.

datasets: Combined Kazakh SPO training corpus comprising limited real data and 10,000 GPT-4-generated synthetic sentences

metrics: Per-class F1 for Subject, Predicate, and Object
Synthetic-corpus quality metric Qa combining Linguistic Consistency Score and Error Rate Reduction
evaluation.setting: Models were trained for 10 epochs with batch size 16, learning rate 5×10^-5, Adam, and dropout 0.1 on an NVIDIA Tesla V100; average training time was about four hours and experiments were repeated several times. The paper does not report corpus provenance, train/dev/test sizes or split procedure.

value: Table 1 reports XLM-RoBERTa at 92.0% precision, 89.5% recall, and 90.73% F1—the highest listed result.
The next-best listed model, BERT with synthetic data, has 83.5% precision, 81.7% recall, and 82.6% F1; BERT without synthetic data has 74.9% F1, BiLSTM-CRF 71.2%, and rules 62.8%.
For XLM-RoBERTa on the combined corpus, the paper additionally reports Subject F1 91.4%, Predicate F1 89.2%, Object F1 91.6%, macro-F1 90.7%, micro-F1 90.9%, and sentence-level exact match 81.3%.
Synthetic-data review found over 90% of sentences conforming to Kazakh norms; agreement on a shared subsample was Cohen's kappa 0.86.

value: Author-stated strength: synthetic augmentation addresses the shortage of annotated Kazakh data and is associated with the highest reported XLM-RoBERTa score.
Author-stated strength: manual and rule-based validation of generated data checks grammar, SPO-span consistency, and cultural/topic bias before training.

Review-level inference: the combination of aggregate, class-level, and sentence exact-match metrics provides a more informative error picture than reporting a single F1 score, although the unspecified data split limits reproducibility.
